thread.title: Apple's iPad Pros And Mac Options Should Leave Investors Scratching Their Heads - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) | Seeking Alpha

author: Michael Henage
title: Apple's iPad Pros And Mac Options Should Leave Investors Scratching Their Heads - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Apple's (NASDAQ: AAPL ) recent revisions to its iPad and Mac lineups are always met with a good bit of press. Most of the articles and reviews have to do with what the company changed or updated. It has never been a secret that Apple's products are targeted at a premium audience. However, the most recent updates seem to have stepped up this game. Apple just took the iPad Pro and the Mac lineup to ultra-premium status. The question investors need to answer, was this the right move for the company's future? In a word... no.
Might as well call it the Pro Plus There was a clear theme among the iPad and Mac releases… better specs equal higher prices. As a quick comparison, last year's iPad Pro 10.5" was priced at $649, the similar 11" model for this year comes in at $799. Though Apple improved the Pro versions by moving to edge-to-edge screens, better components, and USB-C charging, a more than 23% price increase is asking a lot, even for die-hard Apple fans.
On the even higher-end of the spectrum, the larger 12.9" iPad Pro from 2017 was originally priced at $799, whereas the most recent version starts at $999. The justification for these significant price increases seems to be centered around the idea that the iPad Pro is a laptop replacement. It's one thing to convince users to spend $799 to $999 on a tablet, but theoretically putting the iPad Pro head-to-head with laptops is somewhat more palpable.
Walking through some of the comments from Apple about the Pro models, it's clear the tablet market isn't the core focus. Apple says the iPad Pro , "will make you rethink what iPad is capable of" and then in a very coy manner, "and what a computer is capable of." Apple also connects Face ID to this theme, saying "It's the world's most secure facial authentication in a tablet, and in a computer." Last but not least, Apple says of its A12X Bionic chip that "it's faster than most PC laptops."
Slowing demand and higher prices are a real threat The short version of Apple's iPad Pro gamble is very simple: the tablet market isn't enough for the iPad anymore. As far back as 2014, Apple knew the tablet market had problems. At that time, the company reported slowing iPad sales and blamed the problem on "softness in certain parts of the world."
Fast forward to 2016 and tablet sales continued to fall. Moving into this year, studies have confirmed the lengthy upgrade cycle is an issue causing Apple and other tablet manufacturers to suffer. The IDC recently reported the tablet market recorded the 15th straight quarter of declining unit sales.
When it comes to the tablet replacement cycle , as of 2017, it stood at 5.28 years. By 2018, the replacement cycle moved to 5.12 years. According to this year's studies, the replacement cycle by 2022 may drop to 4.78 years, but relative to other devices, this is a very long lead time. If these figures are accurate, Apple may not get a chance to sell a replacement tablet to a user who bought an iPad two years ago, until 2021. This business seems to have morphed into a cyclical industry. Users aren't really looking for a reason to replace their tablet until it dies, or it stops supporting the apps they want to use.
A recent comment by Jitesh Ubrani from IDC seemed to clarify the issue with tablets even further. The comment was, "those operating on tighter budgets have had very few options available to them and hence some have opted for traditional PCs." Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) are trying to address this demand with the Surface Go and Chrome devices, yet Apple just made it more expensive to get arguably the best tablet in the market. Demand for tablets is already very soft; raising prices is a dangerous move.
The iPad isn't like the iPhone. The iPhone has steady if slow demand and is supported by a constant push by carriers to get users to upgrade. Tablet sales have no such assurance or backing. Investors should worry that the company may have just priced itself out of the waning demand it has for the iPad.
Is Apple trying to kill demand in one of its few bright spots in hardware? There have been so many articles devoted to convincing users that we are in a "post-PC era", it's impossible to know where to start. However, recent headlines and studies suggest the death of the PC has been overblown. In 2016, there were 156.8 million total computers sold worldwide. By 2017, this number increased to over 161 million, and by 2018, the total should eclipse 162 million. This same study suggests continued slow growth, to about 165 million units by 2022.
Users are starting to realize there are certain devices that are simply better for certain tasks. A good example is me writing this article. I could theoretically use an iPad or laptop for writing. However, having two screens, and multiple windows open is only possible on a desktop or a laptop connected to a multi-monitor dock.
Users who want to watch videos or play games on a bigger screen likely would favor a tablet over a smartphone, or waiting on a laptop or desktop to boot up. The productivity that is possible only on a desktop or laptop is a solid explanation for why businesses and some consumers are buying PCs. According to IDC and Gartner , the PC industry grew by between 1% and just under 3% this year.
In a similar move to Apple's increased iPad Pro pricing, the company ratcheted up pricing on its cheapest Mac options as well. The MacBook Air that used to be $999 was revamped with a better display and better specs, but at a price 20% higher. In an even more surprising move, the Mac Mini was moved from $499 up to $799. Admittedly, the Mac Mini received significantly better specs, but a price increase of 60%, essentially took Apple out of the mainstream desktop market.
This gets at the core of the concern facing Apple investors. The Mac business generated over $7 billion in revenue last quarter , but that was before the massive price increases. Apple devices have always been premium priced, but it's unclear if users will be willing to pay this much of a premium.

With desktop prices 80% above, and laptop prices more than double that of an average Windows device, Mac is asking users to pony up even more than before. The economic principle of price elasticity suggests consumers will pay more for a good or service, if the price increase isn't so significant that they start to question their purchase decision. Price increases of 20% or more is an obvious difference that consumers will notice.
18% of revenue isn't peanuts The bottom line is Apple seems to be playing with fire. The iPad Pro lineup and the updated Mac lineup cause some confusion as to what Apple is trying to sell its customers. Comparing the MacBook Air to the iPad Pro models suggests Apple's pricing may be about to kill one business while trying to grow the other.

If we look at specs, it seems like the iPad Pro models might be of better value for many users. The MacBook Air is $1,199, yet an iPad Pro 11" with the Smart Keyboard Folio costs $978. The 12.9" with the keyboard would total up to $1,198. The fact that Apple went out of its way to claim, "iPad Pros are faster than 92% of all portable PCs" just further complicates matters.
The combination of iPad and Mac revenue represented 18% of revenue last quarter. While many will focus on iPhone sales or Services growth, risking two of its overlooked revenue streams, with significantly higher prices, is something investors need to pay attention to. The company can't afford missteps, while at the same time calling into question its transparency . The stock is down since the last earnings report, but squashing demand for two struggling businesses is a significant step in the wrong direction.
